title: Ezra 7:1–10
context: “Now after these things” (7:1) moves the story forward from the completion and dedication of the temple in the sixth year of Darius (6:15–22) to the reign of Artaxerxes; the text does not say how much time has passed. Ezra is introduced through a priestly genealogy reaching back to Aaron (7:1–5) and as a skilled scribe in the law of Moses. He travels from Babylon to Jerusalem in four months, arriving in the fifth month of the king’s seventh year, “according to the good hand of his God on him” (7:9), because he had set his heart to seek, do, and teach the LORD’s law (7:10). The genealogy is shorter than the high-priestly line in 1 Chronicles 6:3–14, which lists several more generations between Meraioth and Azariah. Many readers take the shorter list as selective, since “son” can mean descendant and biblical genealogies often skip generations; the text does not explain its selection. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: God’s gracious hand rests on a servant who devotes himself to his word.

verses.text: Now after these things, in the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra the son of Seraiah, the son of Azariah, the son of Hilkiah,
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra is introduced in the reign of Artaxerxes as the son of Seraiah, of the high-priestly line. Arminian readers note that the genealogy establishes Ezra’s standing to teach and lead worship. His heritage gives him a responsibility he will take up with wholehearted devotion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God raises up Ezra from a line he had preserved through exile, linking the restored community to the priesthood God appointed. Shared ground: both traditions read the genealogy as grounding Ezra’s ministry in God’s faithfulness to the priestly line, without pressing the gaps it leaves.

verses.text: the son of Shallum, the son of Zadok, the son of Ahitub,
verses.arminianNotes: Shallum, Zadok, and Ahitub continue Ezra’s line. Arminian readers note the mention of Zadok, whose family served as priests from the time of David and Solomon. Ezra stands in a long tradition of faithful service at God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the Zadokite line and see God’s continuity in the priesthood across the centuries. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical grounding for Ezra’s authority, and neither builds a doctrinal point on the particular names.

verses.text: the son of Amariah, the son of Azariah, the son of Meraioth,
verses.arminianNotes: Amariah, Azariah, and Meraioth are named. Arminian readers note that 1 Chronicles 6:7–10 lists several more generations between Meraioth and Azariah. Ancient genealogies often select names rather than listing every generation, and this one does not explain its choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the shorter list and treat it calmly, since “son” can mean descendant. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of a selective genealogy that establishes Ezra’s priestly descent, without forcing it into exact agreement with 1 Chronicles 6.

verses.text: the son of Zerahiah, the son of Uzzi, the son of Bukki,
verses.arminianNotes: Zerahiah, Uzzi, and Bukki carry the line back toward Aaron. Arminian readers note that these names match the early high-priestly line in 1 Chronicles 6:5–6. The genealogy roots Ezra’s service in the priesthood established in Israel’s earliest days.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the agreement with 1 Chronicles 6 and the continuity of the priestly office. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as genealogical detail that honors God’s preservation of the priesthood, with no theological dispute raised.

verses.text: the son of Abishua, the son of Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the chief priest—
verses.arminianNotes: The line reaches Abishua, Phinehas, Eleazar, and “Aaron the chief priest.” Arminian readers note that Ezra’s ancestry goes back to the first high priest. His ministry continues the calling God gave to Aaron’s family, now renewed after exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the climax of the genealogy in Aaron and recall Phinehas’s zeal for God (Numbers 25:11). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as establishing Ezra’s legitimacy and as testimony that God’s appointed priesthood continued through Israel’s history.

verses.text: this Ezra went up from Babylon. He was a skilled scribe in the law of Moses, which the LORD, the God of Israel, had given; and the king granted him all his request, according to the LORD his God’s hand on him.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra, a skilled scribe in the law of Moses, goes up from Babylon, and the king grants all his request “according to the LORD his God’s hand on him.” Arminian readers note Ezra’s skill and initiative in seeking the king’s support, which God blesses.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s hand as the decisive reason the king grants Ezra’s request, governing a Persian ruler for his people’s good. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as affirming God’s gracious hand on a faithful servant and Ezra’s real diligence in the law, held together without tension.

verses.text: Some of the children of Israel, including some of the priests, the Levites, the singers, the gatekeepers, and the temple servants went up to Jerusalem in the seventh year of Artaxerxes the king.
verses.arminianNotes: Some Israelites, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants go up in the seventh year of Artaxerxes. Arminian readers note that the return is voluntary; people choose to leave Babylon and join the community in Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the range of people who go and see God gathering servants for every role in his house. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing a willing response to God’s work, with each group bringing its own gifts to the restored worship in Jerusalem.

verses.text: He came to Jerusalem in the fifth month, which was in the seventh year of the king.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra arrives in Jerusalem in the fifth month of the king’s seventh year. Arminian readers note the precise dating, which anchors the account in history. The journey is real, with a real beginning and end, and the narrative records it carefully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the careful chronology and see in it the narrator’s concern to show God’s faithfulness at a specific time. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical detail and see no doctrinal question in the date itself.

verses.text: For on the first day of the first month he began to go up from Babylon; and on the first day of the fifth month he came to Jerusalem, according to the good hand of his God on him.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra begins the journey on the first day of the first month and arrives on the first day of the fifth month, “according to the good hand of his God on him.” Arminian readers note the long, demanding journey and see God’s favor accompanying a faithful traveler.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the phrase as a confession that the safe arrival was God’s gift, not merely the result of good planning. Shared ground: both traditions read the good hand of God as gracious, providential care, and both treat it as common ground rather than a point of dispute.

verses.text: For Ezra had set his heart to seek the LORD’s law, and to do it, and to teach statutes and ordinances in Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra had set his heart to seek the LORD’s law, to do it, and to teach it. Arminian readers stress the order: study, obedience, then teaching. Ezra’s wholehearted devotion is a real response to God’s word and a model for every believer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise commend Ezra’s devotion and note that “for” links it to God’s good hand in 7:9, while seeing such a heart as itself a gift of grace. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a model of seeking, doing, and teaching God’s word, with God’s favor and human devotion held together.
